family: Not a single alphabet: an author-and-books item. It covers the books in which Trithemius carried cipher and secret alphabets into manuscript and print (the Steganographia, begun 1499 and printed 1606; the Polygraphia, a manuscript version presented to Maximilian in 1508 and printed in July 1518), Agrippa's visit and the exchange over the draft of De occulta philosophia (reply dated 8 April 1510), and the Golden Dawn Cipher Manuscripts (brought forward 1887), written in English in a Trithemian cipher alphabet keyed to the Latin letters. The two alphabets this file treats (the Theban table he ascribes to Honorius, and the Golden Dawn cipher) are keyed to the Latin letters, not to the Hebrew like the ring-letter alphabets of Agrippa III.30. The rest of the Polygraphia's catalogue has not been inventoried, so no claim is made about all of it.
summary: Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), Benedictine abbot of Sponheim and, from 1506, of St Jakob at Würzburg, wrote two of the founding books of early modern secret writing. His Steganographia (begun 1499 and left unfinished; printed at Frankfurt in 1606; placed on the Index in 1609) hides cipher methods under conjurations of angels and spirits; its Book III was publicly solved as cipher only in 1996–98, although Heidel had solved it in 1676 and printed his answer in a cipher of his own. His Polygraphia, presented in manuscript to Maximilian in 1508 and printed after his death in July 1518, is commonly called the first printed book on cryptography; it has word tables (the so-called 'Ave Maria' cipher), a square table (tabula recta) and a catalogue of alphabets that includes one he ascribes to 'Honorius surnamed the Theban'. Agrippa visited him at Würzburg and then sent him the draft of De occulta philosophia, to which he replied on 8 April 1510; in 1887 Westcott brought forward the Golden Dawn's Cipher Manuscripts, written in English in a cipher alphabet taken from Trithemius.

firstAttestation.work: Polygraphiae libri sex Ioannis Trithemii abbatis Peapolitani, quondam Spanheimensis, ad Maximilianum Caesarem
firstAttestation.author: Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), abbot of Sponheim, then from 1506 abbot of St Jakob (the Schottenkloster) at Würzburg (GND record and SEP, as reported by theban.verified.json (a search-backed sibling fact-check of this session)). The Graecising etymology of 'Peapolis' (from Herbipolis) is the researcher's gloss and is not verified.
firstAttestation.date: July 1518 (printing, posthumous). The Library of Congress record transcribes the imprint as 'anno a Christo nato MDXVIII men. Iulio'; the Folger record as 'anno MDXVIII mense Iulio'; the UVaDoc record notes two colophons and takes its data from the second, at sig. C3v (all as reported by theban.verified.json (a search-backed sibling fact-check of this session); the research file's '1518 mense Iulio' was a loose transcription). Trithemius died in December 1516 (13 December by the fact-checker's knowledge; not verified here). Composition: an NSA Center for Cryptologic History pamphlet says he BEGAN it at Würzburg in 1508; German Wikipedia says he COMPLETED it in 1508; the publisher's description of Maximilian Gamer's edition (Brill, 2022) says he dedicated a first, manuscript version to Maximilian I in 1508 and handed over an autograph (all as reported by theban.verified.json (a search-backed sibling fact-check of this session)). The research file credited 'begun in 1508' to the Library of Congress; the theban fact-check did not find it in the LoC record, so that attribution is withdrawn.
firstAttestation.place: Basel or Oppenheim; the sources disagree. The colophon names the bookseller Johannes Haselberg 'de Aia', of the diocese of Constance, at whose cost it was printed; the Folger record says he was active at Reichenau 1515–1537. Folger gives the printing chiefly to Michael Furter of Basel, but also records that Furter died between 5 March and 2 May 1517, over a year before the July 1518 colophon; it lists Panzer, Brunet, Grässe, Caillet, LC and Shulman for Oppenheim, and Isaac, Dodgson, BM STC and Wellcome for Adam Petri, Basel. Wellcome reads '[Basle]: A. Petri'; the Metropolitan Museum names Adam Petri; a Christie's lot gives Oppenheim, Jakob Köbel; the current LoC record gives Basel; UVaDoc reports ICCU placing Haselberg in Basel in 1518–19. Woodcuts: the Met credits Hans Springinklee, but the Folger notes that Dodgson gives the title woodcut to Springinklee and M. Lankorońska (Gutenberg-Jahrbuch 1955) to an artist of Burgkmair's workshop. All as reported by theban.verified.json (a search-backed sibling fact-check of this session); not re-seen here.
firstAttestation.locator: Whole work (printed 1518). The book, folio and signature of the alphabet catalogue in the 1518 printing are NOT verified, and the sources conflict. (a) Peterson (The Sworn Book of Honorius, introduction) cites the Theban passage as 'Polygraphia 6, 1508, p. 579', i.e. Book VI. (b) Wikipedia cites p. 597. Neither can be a page of the 1518 printing, which is unpaginated (about 255–270 leaves by the Pandolfini, UVaDoc and ABAA collations); they fit a paginated later edition such as Zetzner's Strasbourg octavo of 1600 (612 pp.) or its 1613 reprint (an inference from the collations, reported by theban.verified.json (a search-backed sibling fact-check of this session)). (c) In the 1561 French translation the Theban page is fol. 184v; a Wikipedia talk-page editor places it in Book V, which the theban fact-check could not confirm, and in any case the French arrangement does not settle the 1518 Latin book number. (d) The ABAA description's 'Book V' could not be seen in a snippet by the theban fact-check. Book V or VI stays open.
firstAttestation.notes: This is the first PRINTED attestation of a Trithemian cipher alphabet, so far as the sources seen report (an inference from the absence of any earlier printing in them). It may not be the first attestation: the 1508 autograph manuscript of the Polygraphia given to Maximilian (critical edition by Maximilian Gamer, Brill, 2022) was not checked for the catalogue of alphabets or the Theban table, and the Steganographia (begun 1499) circulated in manuscript for a century. Trithemius's secret-writing project is mentioned earlier, in his letter of 1499 to the Carmelite Arnold Bostius announcing the Steganographia (researcher's and fact-checker's knowledge, not verified; the fact-checker recalls 25 March 1499). The Steganographia itself was not printed until 1606 (house timeline).

claims.claim: Trithemius began the Steganographia in 1499 and left it unfinished.
claims.evidence: Stated in the house timeline. His own letter to Bostius of 1499 announces the work (prior knowledge, not verified in this run). It was printed only in 1606.
sources: Brann 1999 (prior knowledge, not verified in this run)

claims.claim: The Steganographia is a book of angel magic.
claims.evidence: The surface is conjuration: spirits with barbarous names are invoked to carry messages. The conjurations of Books I and II were long understood to be cipher systems, and Book III was publicly solved as cipher in 1996–98 (Heidel had solved it in 1676). Brann and others hold that this does not dispose of the angels: Trithemius may have meant a real angelic magic and a real cipher at once, and he disowned neither reading (house timeline). The page should give both readings and endorse neither.
sources: Noel L. Brann, Trithemius and Magical Theology (1999), not consulted

claims.claim: The conjurations of Steganographia Books I and II conceal cipher messages.
claims.evidence: The house timeline says so. Heidel (1676) and, by prior knowledge, not verified in this run, the Clavis printed with the 1606 edition and Selenus (1624) expound the methods. As I recall it, the 'barbarous' words mostly carry nulls, and the letters that count are picked out by a rule; I have not checked a worked example.
sources: Heidel 1676; Selenus 1624 (prior knowledge, not verified in this run)

claims.claim: Book III's planetary-angel tables were solved by Thomas Ernst (1996) and independently by Jim Reeds (1998), and had already been solved by Heidel in 1676.
claims.evidence: Stated in the house timeline. The Heidel point is Ernst's finding: Heidel printed his solution in a cipher of his own.

claims.claim: The Polygraphia (1518) is the first printed book on cryptography.
claims.evidence: The house timeline calls it 'the first printed book of cryptography in Europe'. History of Information heads its entry 'Johannes Trithemius Issues the First Book on Cryptography' (as reported by the theban fact-check). It is posthumous, printed in July 1518. Present it as the usual description: Alberti's De componendis cifris (c. 1466) is older but was not printed in his lifetime (fact-checker's knowledge, not verified).

Trithemius does not claim it. He ascribes it to 'Honorius cognomento Thebanus' and cites Pietro d'Abano's 'greater fourth book' as his witness (Latin as quoted by Peterson). Peterson says he could not identify any such passage in d'Abano's works, and no copy earlier than 1518 is known to the sources consulted (theban fact-check), though the 1508 manuscript Polygraphia was not checked. Agrippa III.29 repeats the ascription without naming Trithemius ('which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes', 1651 English, p. 438, checked). The page should report Trithemius's ascription, and the open question whether he made the alphabet himself, without settling it.
sources: Trithemius, Polygraphia (1518), via Peterson and Wikipedia (theban.verified.json)
Agrippa, Three Books of Occult Philosophy (1651), III.29, p. 438 (EEBO-TCP A26565, checked)

claims.claim: The 'Frankish' letters that Trithemius gives on the authority of the chronicler Hunibald are ancient.
claims.evidence: By prior knowledge, not verified in this run: Trithemius cites a sixth-century Frankish historian, 'Hunibald', whom no one else attests, and scholars (Klaus Arnold; Brann) generally take Hunibald to be Trithemius's own invention. I believe the Polygraphia's catalogue includes letters credited to the Franks, but I could not confirm this or any locator in this run. Do not display such a table until it is checked.
sources: Klaus Arnold, Johannes Trithemius (1971; 2nd ed. 1991), not consulted

claims.evidence: Popular accounts, including Wikipedia, call Agrippa his student. The documented contact is Agrippa's stay at Würzburg in the winter of 1509–10 (SEP, as reported) and the exchange of the draft and the reply of 8 April 1510, both letters checked in the 1651 English. Agrippa's own words are 'for a while conversant with you in your Monastery of Herbipolis'. Write 'Agrippa visited Trithemius and sent him his draft', not 'his pupil'.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa' (as reported by theban.verified.json)
Agrippa, Three Books of Occult Philosophy (1651), front matter (EEBO-TCP A26565, checked)

claims.claim: Agrippa sent Trithemius the draft of De occulta philosophia, and Trithemius replied on 8 April 1510.

The reply is headed 'John Tritemius, Abbot of Saint James of Herbipolis, formerly of Spanhemia, to his Henry Cornelius Agrippa of Nettes-heym, health and love', says the work was 'sent by this bearer', and is dated 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.' (the research file's remembered 'An. MDX' is corrected). The draft is reported to survive as Würzburg UB, M. ch. q. 50, and Perrone Compagni's edition takes account of it (sibling research; not seen).

claims.claim: Trithemius is the 'father' of the secret alphabets.
claims.evidence: This is a modern epithet. Invented signs and cipher alphabets are far older: there are charaktêres in late-antique magic (charakteres sibling), and medieval manuscripts collected alphabets. What is documented is narrower: his Polygraphia is commonly called the first printed book on cryptography, and it printed a catalogue of alphabets, real and attributed, which Agrippa and later authors drew on (for the Theban, by inference from the agreement of the texts). By prior knowledge, not verified in this run, the word 'steganography' derives from the title of his book.

claims.claim: Trithemius wrote a treatise for the Emperor Maximilian on the seven planetary intelligences that govern the world in turn.
claims.evidence: Agrippa III.24 names the intelligences (Oriphiel, Zachariel, Zamael, Michael, Anael, Raphael, Gabriel), says each governs the world 354 years and four months in the order Saturn, Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Moon, Sun, and adds 'Abbas Tritemius writ to Maximilian Caesar a speciall Treatise concerning these' (1651 English, p. 416, checked). uses.use: Hiding a message inside an innocent-looking devotional Latin text

uses.use: Hiding a message under a conjuration of spirits

uses.use: Polyalphabetic encipherment with an alphabet that shifts at every letter

letters.name: Steganographia (begun 1499; printed Frankfurt, 1606; Index 1609)
letters.form: Not a glyph. A book card with two layers, the surface and what lies beneath. The surface has three books: Books I–II conjure spirits with barbarous names to carry messages, and Book III invokes the seven planetary angels with tables of numbers. Beneath, all three are cipher systems. Give the dates: begun 1499, left unfinished, printed 1606, Index 1609. Then the decipherers: Heidel 1676, Ernst 1996, Reeds 1998.
letters.note: The dates and decipherers are from the house timeline. The description of each book's contents is prior knowledge, not verified in this run. The 1606 printer, publisher and full title are unverified.

letters.name: Steganographia, Books I–II: the conjurations
letters.form: Not a glyph. A card naming a few of the spirits (as I recall it, Book I opens with Pamersiel, Padiel and Camuel) and showing the principle: most letters of the incantation are nulls, and the significant letters are picked by a rule. Do NOT print a worked decipherment unless it has been checked against the 1606 text, the 1606 Clavis or Heidel (1676).
letters.note: The spirit names and the mechanism are prior knowledge, not verified in this run. By the same knowledge, the Ars Theurgia-Goetia of the Lemegeton takes over these spirits; Peterson's introduction to The Lesser Key of Solomon (2001) is where to check this.

letters.name: Steganographia, Book III: the planetary angels and their tables
letters.form: Not a glyph. A card: seven planetary angels, tables of numbers, centuries of being read as pure magic, then the solutions. Ernst broke it in 1996 and Reeds independently in 1998, finding ordinary Latin. Heidel had solved it in 1676 and printed his answer in a cipher of his own.
letters.note: The solutions and Heidel's encrypted answer are from the house timeline. The article titles and journals (Daphnis 25; Cryptologia 22) are prior knowledge, not verified in this run. The identification of Book III's angels with the seven intelligences of the treatise to Maximilian is prior knowledge, not verified. Agrippa III.24 (1651, p. 416, checked) names those seven as Oriphiel (Saturn), Zachariel (Jupiter), Zamael (Mars), Michael (Sun), Anael (Venus), Raphael (Mercury) and Gabriel (Moon); note 'Zamael', where the research file wrote 'Samael'. Do not print Book III's own spellings until seen.

letters.name: Polygraphiae libri sex (written about 1508; printed July 1518)
letters.form: Not a glyph. A book card: six books and a key, dedicated to the Emperor Maximilian ('ad Maximilianum Caesarem'), a first manuscript version presented to him in 1508, printed posthumously in July 1518 at the expense of Johannes Haselberg 'de Aia'. Place and printer disputed (Basel: Furter or Adam Petri; Oppenheim: Jakob Köbel); Furter died in 1517. The title woodcut is credited to Hans Springinklee by the Met and Dodgson, and to Burgkmair's workshop by Lankorońska. Copies: Library of Congress (Fabyan collection), Folger, Wellcome, Valladolid.
letters.note: FACT-CHECK: lowered from high. The bibliographic facts are catalogue reports relayed by the theban fact-check (LoC, Folger, UVaDoc, Wellcome, Met, Christie's, Gamer/Brill); not re-seen in this check. The place, the printer, the woodcut attribution and 'begun' versus 'completed' 1508 remain open, so the card must show them as disputes. 'And a key' rests on a bookseller's description and on UVaDoc's two colophons (inference).

letters.name: Polygraphia, Book I: the 'Ave Maria' word tables
letters.form: Not a glyph. A table card showing one column of the word tables (one Latin word per letter of Trithemius's 24-letter alphabet) and a short enciphered phrase, so the reader sees ciphertext that reads as a prayer. As I recall the first column (Kahn 1967, from memory; DO NOT DISPLAY until checked against the 1518 Book I): a Deus, b Creator, c Conditor, d Opifex, e Dominus, f Dominator, g Consolator, h Arbiter, i Iudex, k Illuminator, l Illustrator, m Rector, n Rex, o Imperator, p Gubernator, q Factor, r Fabricator, s Conservator, t Redemptor, u Auctor, x Princeps, y Pastor, z Moderator, w Salvator.
letters.note: The number of columns (384, as recalled), the word list and the source of the name 'Ave Maria' are all prior knowledge, not verified in this run. The fact-checker's own recollection of Kahn agrees with the first column given, but that is memory against memory, not a check. The contents of Books II–IV are not described here.

letters.name: Polygraphia: the tabula recta (Book V by recollection; unverified)
letters.form: Not a glyph. A 24 × 24 square of Trithemius's Latin alphabet (a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x y z w), each row shifted one place to the left. The writer enciphers letter 1 with row 1, letter 2 with row 2, and so on. It can be generated rather than drawn, but the letter order must be checked against the 1518 page first.
letters.note: FACT-CHECK: lowered from medium, because a generated square inherits an unverified letter order. The book number (V), the 24-letter order with w last and the progressive use are prior knowledge, not verified in this run (Kahn 1967). The 1518 Theban table's final sign labelled 'w' (reported by a Wikipedia talk-page editor and From Old Books, via the theban fact-check) fits the 24-letter scheme but does not prove the tabula recta's order.

letters.name: Polygraphia: the catalogue of alphabets (Book V or VI)
letters.form: Not a glyph. An index card listing the alphabets printed in the catalogue, each as Trithemius labels it, with its attribution reported as an attribution. The only entry verified here is the Theban, which he ascribes to 'Honorius surnamed the Theban' on Pietro d'Abano's testimony; it links to the theban page. The remaining entries are to be inventoried from the 1518 woodcuts.
letters.note: The book number is disputed: V for the 1561 French (talk page; unconfirmed) and per ABAA (unconfirmed), VI per Peterson. By prior knowledge, not verified in this run, the catalogue also holds alphabets credited to the ancient Franks (on the authority of 'Hunibald', whom scholars take to be Trithemius's own fiction) and others, some of his own devising; the runes sibling also suspects a 'Norman' alphabet. None of this is verified, so do not list them until the 1518 pages have been seen.

letters.form: Not a glyph. A book card: the first French translation, by Gabriel de Collange, printed by Benoît Prévost for Jacques Kerver, Paris, 1561. Its Theban page is fol. 184v; its heading names Honorius 'surnamed Thebanus' and drops d'Abano.
letters.note: FACT-CHECK: lowered from high. The imprint (Sotheby's, Tomash lot 669), the folio and the heading (Wikimedia Commons, BPL copy) are as reported by the theban fact-check; not re-seen here. letters.name: Agrippa's draft and Trithemius's reply (Würzburg, 8 April 1510)
letters.form: Not a glyph. A card for the encounter. Agrippa stays at St Jakob, Würzburg, in the winter of 1509–10 ('for a while conversant with you in your Monastery of Herbipolis') and afterwards sends the draft of De occulta philosophia with a dedicatory letter ('which you have sent by this bearer'). Trithemius replies 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.': praise, and the rule to keep higher secrets for higher friends ('Give Hey to an Ox, Sugar to a Parret only', 1651 English). The draft is reported to survive as Würzburg UB, M. ch. q. 50, and Perrone Compagni's edition (1992) takes account of it. Both letters are in the 1651 English front matter.
letters.note: FACT-CHECK: the quotation and 'sent by this bearer' are now checked against the 1651 English (EEBO-TCP A26565); the remembered 'Give hay to an Ox, sugar to a Parrot' was wrong in wording. 'Both letters were printed in 1533' is the fact-checker's knowledge, not checked against the 1533 Latin. The shelfmark is reported, not seen. Whether the draft held the secret alphabets is an open question: say so on the card. The house timeline's 'brought him a manuscript' differs from the letter's 'sent by this bearer'.

letters.name: The Golden Dawn Cipher Manuscripts (brought forward 1887)
letters.form: Not a glyph. A card: a set of ritual outlines in English, enciphered with a Trithemian alphabet. Westcott brought them forward in 1887, and Mathers worked them up into the grade rituals of the Golden Dawn (opened 1888). Their author and date are unknown; some later accounts trace them to Kenneth Mackenzie's papers. A note found with them is reported to give a Stuttgart address for 'Anna Sprengel' (the story more usually gives Nuremberg), and the Sprengel letters are judged forgeries (Howe 1972; Gilbert). Show the cipher alphabet (the units below), but not the ritual text.
letters.note: The core facts are from the house (rosicrucian.js, esoteric.js, themes/latin.js). The folio count (60 in Wikipedia, as I recall it), the 1809 watermark, Woodford and Hockley, the five grades, and Küntz's 1996 facsimile edition are all prior knowledge, not verified in this run. The present location of the manuscripts is not established here.

lettersSource: NOT A SINGLE ALPHABET. Units 1–11 are the works and documents the page should show as cards. For these, 'form' says what the card holds, and 'formConfidence' grades the card's facts, since there is nothing to draw. Units 12–35 are the cipher alphabet of the Golden Dawn Cipher Manuscripts, keyed to the Latin letters. ORDER AND VALUES: assumed to be Trithemius's 24-letter alphabet, a–z without j and v and with w last (prior knowledge, not verified in this run; consistent with the 1518 Theban table's final sign, reported as labelled 'w' by the theban fact-check). FORMS: NONE SEEN, and all 24 are marked NOT DESCRIBED. Trace them from the facsimile in Küntz (ed.), The Complete Golden Dawn Cipher Manuscript (1996), and check them against the Trithemian source table. That table is still to be identified: it is probably one of the alphabets in the Polygraphia's catalogue (Library of Congress Fabyan copy of 1518; 1561 French, BPL copy, on the Internet Archive and Wikimedia Commons). Do not draw from modern fonts, cipher-tool websites or charts that give no edition. Do not borrow the forms of Theban, Malachim or any other alphabet by analogy. FACT-CHECK: units 1, 5, 7 and 9 had their card confidence lowered; the 24 cipher signs stay NOT DESCRIBED.
cautions: BASIS. The researcher worked after the session's shared web-search budget had run out, and so did this fact-check (its first search was refused; WebFetch failed with 'getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND'). Statements are marked by basis: checked in the 1651 English (EEBO-TCP A26565, read locally); house data (checked in the site's files); reported by the search-backed theban fact-check (theban.verified.json); sibling research; or prior knowledge, not verified. Nothing in the last class should be printed as fact until checked.
LETTER FORMS ARE NOT DESCRIBED. Drawing 'the Golden Dawn cipher' from this file would mean inventing it. Trace the signs from the Küntz facsimile and the Trithemian source table, or show a gap.

Do not write 'Trithemius invented the Theban alphabet' or 'Honorius of Thebes invented it'. Write that Trithemius ascribes it to Honorius surnamed the Theban, citing Pietro d'Abano, that Agrippa repeats the ascription without naming Trithemius, and that no copy earlier than 1518 is known to the sources consulted (the 1508 manuscript Polygraphia has not been checked).

Do not call Agrippa Trithemius's pupil. The documented contact is the stay at Würzburg in the winter of 1509–10 and the exchange of letters (reply dated 8 April 1510). Do not say the 1510 draft contained the alphabets: that is unverified. The 1651 reply says the draft was 'sent by this bearer'; the house timeline's 'brought' should be checked against Perrone Compagni or SEP.

Give both readings of the Steganographia, cipher manual and angel magic, and endorse neither. The house timeline's wording, that Brann holds the cryptography 'does not dispose of the angels', is the model.
'Ave Maria cipher' is a later label for the Polygraphia Book I tables. Present it as a name, not as Trithemius's own title, unless the 1518 text is shown to use it.

Do not give the Polygraphia's alphabets a book number as settled. Sources differ between Book V (1561 French, per a Wikipedia talk page; ABAA) and Book VI (Peterson). Do not give Peterson's p. 579 or Wikipedia's p. 597 as 1518 pages: the 1518 printing is unpaginated.

Do not date the Steganographia to 1606, and do not date the Polygraphia to 1508 as if printed then. Say 'begun 1499, printed 1606' and 'a manuscript version presented to Maximilian in 1508, printed July 1518'. Do not credit the 'begun 1508' claim to the Library of Congress.

Golden Dawn: show the cipher alphabet, which is Trithemius's, and the history. Do not reproduce the ritual text of the Cipher Manuscripts or the later Golden Dawn rituals worked up from them, which living orders use, or any living order's emblems. Report the Sprengel story as Westcott's account, and the forgery as the conclusion of Howe and Gilbert.
Sprengel's city. The house places the address on the note at Stuttgart, but the story usually gives Nuremberg (house rosicrucian.js). Keep to the house wording.

Hunibald and the 'Frankish' letters: if the page mentions them, call Hunibald a source cited only by Trithemius and generally judged his invention. Do not display the letters until the 1518 page has been checked.
Ritual use is reported neutrally. The Steganographia's spirits passed into the Ars Theurgia-Goetia; say so as history, without mockery and without endorsement.

The 1651 English renders Trithemius's title as 'a Neapolitanian Abbot'. That is a slip for Peapolitanus (the Würzburg house), not Naples; the same front matter heads his letter 'Abbot of Saint James of Herbipolis' and dates it from 'our Monastery of Peapolis'.

Printer and woodcuts of 1518: the Folger itself records that Michael Furter died in spring 1517, which tells against a printing 'chiefly' by him in July 1518; and the Springinklee attribution of the title woodcut is contested (Lankorońska: Burgkmair's workshop). Report both as disputes.

Agrippa III.24 (1651, p. 416) is the one checked primary witness to Trithemius's treatise on the seven intelligences. Spell the names as the source being quoted spells them (Agrippa 1651 has 'Oriphiel' and 'Zamael').
